chunks: "There are three reasons, from hardest to softest. The hardest is the reticle limit .
The lithography scanner exposes the mask pattern in a field of about 26 by 33 millimetres, which is about 858 square millimetres, so a die can't normally be bigger than that.
Making a larger chip needs stitching several exposures together, which is only done in special cases. The second is yield and cost .
Random defects kill a die in proportion to its area: with Poisson statistics, yield is e to the minus area times defect density. At 0.
1 defects per square centimetre, a 100 square millimetre die yields about 90 percent, but an 858 square millimetre die about 42 percent.
And fewer big dies fit on a 300 millimetre wafer, about 59 instead of 640.
On a ten-thousand-dollar wafer that's about 17 dollars per good small die versus about 400 for the reticle-sized one.
The third is physical design: delivering hundreds of amps, distributing a clock across a huge area, removing heat, and wires that are long and slow.
The workarounds are mostly about breaking the die up.

Chiplets : build several smaller dies, which have much better yield, test them before assembly, and connect them in one package using a silicon interposer, bridge or organic substrate with very short, wide links.

Splitting an 858 square millimetre design into four chiplets, each a quarter of the area plus about 10 percent for the die-to-die interfaces, gives dies of about 236 square millimetres at roughly 79 percent yield, and the silicon costs around half as much as the single big die in my example.
Second, redundancy : spare cores, memory rows and routing around defects.

The extreme case is wafer-scale, where a company builds a chip as big as the wafer, 46,000 square millimetres, out of hundreds of thousands of tiny cores, with enough spares and reconfigurable routing that a few dozen defects don't matter.
The price is the packaging, power and cooling for something that size, and the cost of the die-to-die link, which is slower and more energy-hungry than on-die wires."
